model.economic_buyer: Usually the go-to-market side, sales leadership and revenue ops, not the general counsel. Crosby says outright it was built by lawyers for sales teams to speed up time to signature (crosby.ai, 2026). A contract stuck in review is booked revenue that hasn't landed, which means the budget comes out of a cost-of-delay line, not a legal line. Heads of legal buy too, but as capacity relief rather than headcount.
model.emotional_driver: The deal is sitting there. Not fear of a bad clause, fear of the quarter slipping while a firm takes six weeks to redline an NDA. Fixed price plus a stated turnaround removes both the legal anxiety and the invoice anxiety in one purchase.
model.recurring_vs_one_time: Priced one-time per document, but behaves like a subscription because contract flow is continuous. A company doing dozens of NDAs, MSAs and DPAs a month becomes a de facto recurring account. The 30% monthly growth in GTM teams compounds on top of existing accounts (Crosby Journal, 2025).
model.margins: Not disclosed, but the structure is clear. Cost per document is attorney minutes plus inference; revenue per document is fixed. AI handles the first pass, the attorney reviews and takes liability, so every minute shaved drops to contribution margin. Unlike a traditional firm, getting faster does not shrink the invoice. The offsetting cost is real: 50+ barred attorneys and malpractice insurance are fixed overhead, so utilization is everything.
model.capital_to_start: Crosby raised $80M across two rounds because it is building agents, a client platform and a lateral-hire attorney bench (Crosby Journal, 2025 and 2026). A one-person version of the same archetype needs $2K-$15K: an LLC, a landing page with a published price and turnaround, off-the-shelf AI, and a licensed professional on contract for whatever requires a license. The capital buys credibility and coverage, not tooling.
model.moat: Three layers. One, it is a law firm that carries liability and malpractice insurance, which a software vendor legally cannot do. Two, negotiation history: it claims data from negotiating against 76% of the Fortune 100, so it knows which redlines get accepted and which stall a deal (crosby.ai, 2026). Three, brand reference accounts like Cursor and Clay. Layer one is the real barrier, because pure software competitors have to tell customers to get a lawyer to check the output.
model.distribution: Founder-led sales into the fast-growing AI and software cluster, then referral inside that network. Public case studies with recognizable logos do the selling. Cooley LLP and Patrick Collison investing in the Series A is distribution disguised as capital (Crosby Journal, 2025).

data.why_it_works: The billable hour taxes competence: if you double your speed you halve your invoice, so no law firm has a financial reason to industrialize. Crosby breaks that by fixing the price to the document instead of the clock, which turns every minute of AI leverage into margin rather than a discount. Because the scope is deliberately narrow (NDAs, MSAs, DPAs), the same document shapes repeat thousands of times, so each review makes the next one faster and more predictable, which is what lets them promise hours instead of weeks. That promise is what the buyer is actually paying for, and because the buyer is the revenue team rather than legal, the comparison is not a cheaper lawyer, it is a faster close. Then the firm structure, barred attorneys and malpractice insurance, lets the client fully offload the work instead of babysitting a tool, which is why volume scaled from 1,000 contracts in 173 days to 1,000 every three weeks.

how_to_start.first_step: Pick the single most repetitive deliverable in a field you know, then publish the two things incumbents refuse to publish: one price and one turnaround time. This week, write a one-page offer with exact inclusions and exclusions, take it to five people who currently buy that work hourly, and ask what turnaround would make them switch. Deliver the first twenty by hand and document every step, because the process notes are the product.
how_to_start.hardest_part: Variance, and then liability. On a fixed fee, one messy job eats the profit from three clean ones, so copycats die from scope creep they were too polite to refuse. And the moment you sell an outcome rather than hours, you own the downside: Crosby carries full malpractice insurance and takes liability for its work, which is exactly the expensive, unglamorous part imitators skip.

data.takeaway: If you bill by the hour, getting better at your job lowers your income. Fix the price to a tightly defined outcome and every efficiency you find becomes margin instead of a smaller invoice, which is the only way a service business gets software-like economics.

data.audio_script:
This is The Daily Teardown for Thursday, September seventeenth, twenty twenty-six. Today's archetype: productized service.

Here's the hook. America's hundred biggest law firms made sixty-nine billion dollars in profit last year, and every cent of it was paid out to partners as compensation. That's not my number, that's the number Crosby's founders opened their own funding announcement with in March of twenty twenty-six. And it tells you exactly what they're attacking.

Crosby is a law firm. Not legal software, an actual registered law firm with more than fifty licensed attorneys, malpractice insurance, and liability for its own work. What it does is narrow on purpose. Commercial contracts. Non-disclosure agreements, master service agreements, data processing addenda. The boring paper that sits between a handshake and money in the bank. AI agents do the first pass, a barred attorney signs off, and according to the company's own Series A post from October twenty twenty-five, more than ninety percent of documents go back in a few hours. Their clients are the fast-growing software companies you'd expect... Cursor, Clay, Gumloop. One customer put it bluntly on Crosby's site, saying Crosby did in twelve hours what a really great law firm took six weeks to do.

Before I tell you... take a guess. Who actually pays, and how does the money flow? I'll give you a second.

...

Here it is. The buyer usually isn't the general counsel. It's the go-to-market side of the house, sales and revenue operations, because a contract stuck in review is a signed deal that hasn't turned into cash yet. And the money doesn't flow by the hour. Crosby's own site says it in five words: fixed rates by the document. Don't buy hours, buy outcomes. That is the entire archetype in one line.

Now the numbers, and they're all from Crosby's own posts, so treat them as founder-stated. When they launched publicly in June of twenty twenty-five, their thousandth contract had taken a hundred and seventy-three days. By October, they were doing a thousand every three weeks. Do the arithmetic and that's roughly forty-eight documents a day, call it seventeen thousand a year at that pace. They also said thirty percent more go-to-market teams were signing on each month. On the funding side, twenty million dollars in October twenty-five from Index, Bain Capital Ventures and Elad Gil, with Sequoia, the law firm Cooley, and Patrick Collison participating. Then sixty million dollars in March twenty twenty-six, led by Lux and Index. Eighty million within a year of coming out of stealth, for a business that bills flat fees on paperwork.

Why does this work? Because the hourly model punishes speed. If you get twice as fast on a billable clock, you invoice half as much. Flip to a fixed price per document and speed becomes margin. The AI first pass cuts the minutes per contract, the price stays the same, and the gap is yours. Better still, repetition compounds. An NDA looks like every other NDA, so every review teaches the system which redlines get accepted and which ones stall a deal. Crosby claims it has negotiated against seventy-six percent of the Fortune One Hundred, which is a data asset no individual lawyer accumulates.

Where else does this show up? Superside sells creative work as a flat monthly subscription instead of an agency estimate. Pilot sells startup bookkeeping as a fixed monthly fee instead of an accountant's hourly rate. Same trick, different paper.

How would you start one? Pick one document, one deliverable, one repeatable thing people currently buy in vague hourly chunks. Publish two things a normal firm refuses to publish: a price and a turnaround time. Then deliver the first twenty by hand and write down every step, because your process notes are the actual product.

The hardest part is not the delivery, it's the variance. Fixed price means the ugly job eats the profit from three clean ones, so you need scope so tight it's almost boring, and the discipline to say no to anything outside it. And if you're selling an outcome, you're also buying the liability. Crosby carries malpractice insurance for exactly that reason. That's the part copycats skip.

The takeaway. Charging by the hour caps you at your calendar and taxes you for getting good. Charge a fixed price for a fixed outcome, and every minute you shave turns into margin instead of a smaller invoice.

That's the teardown. See you tomorrow.
